transcript.content: Hello, thank you for coming in. Can you tell me what’s been bothering you or what brings you here today?

I’m here because I… I keep blowing up at people, and it’s scaring me a little. It’s over things that are so small, things I would normally just handle or correct calmly. Like at work, one of my employees put stock on the wrong shelf, and I just snapped. I yelled at them — really yelled — and as soon as it was happening I could almost hear myself, like, “Why are you reacting like this?” But I couldn’t seem to stop it in the moment.

Afterward I was shaking, and I felt awful, because that’s not how I usually treat people. I’ve worked retail a long time, I know shelves get messed up, people make mistakes, especially when it’s busy. Normally I’d just say, “Hey, this goes over here,” and move on. But lately it’s like the smallest thing sets me off, and I’m angry before I even understand why. That’s really what made me think I needed to come in.
Outside of these specific moments where you snap at people, do you find yourself feeling irritable or angry most of the time?

Yes… I think so, but it’s hard to separate it from those blowups because it feels like I’m sort of on edge underneath everything. Like, I don’t walk around thinking, “I’m angry,” all day, but then something tiny happens — something completely ordinary, like the stock being on the wrong shelf — and it’s like it hits some nerve I didn’t even know was exposed.

And the yelling at my employee really shook me because that’s not me. I mean, I’m a manager in retail, things get misplaced constantly. That’s just part of the job. Normally I’d correct it and move on, maybe be mildly annoyed, but lately I go from zero to furious so fast. Then afterward I’m shaking and embarrassed and thinking, “Why did I do that over nothing?” So… I guess yes, there’s a lot more irritability there than usual, even if I don’t always recognize it until I’ve already snapped.
Have you been dealing with any other stressful situations or changes in your life recently that might be contributing to how you’re feeling?

Yes. It started about two weeks ago, and it’s been pretty much since the kitchen fire. It happened during our first weekend working on the house, so it wasn’t just a normal stressful weekend or anything like that.

We’d just started trying to get things done there, and then the fire happened in the kitchen, and ever since then I feel like I haven’t really gone back to normal. I keep thinking, “It’s only been two weeks, maybe I should be handling it better,” but it’s been like a switch flipped after that weekend. That’s when all of this really started — the irritability, the snapping, just feeling like I’m not myself.
Since the fire, have you noticed any changes in your mood besides irritability and anger—like feeling sad, hopeless, or losing interest in things you usually enjoy?

I don’t really know. I mean… I wouldn’t say I feel hopeless, exactly. It’s more like I feel wound up and unsettled, if that makes sense. I haven’t sat there thinking, “Everything is pointless,” or anything like that.

As for sad… maybe a little upset sometimes when I think about the fire, but I don’t know if I’d call it sadness the way you’re asking. It’s more like I get tense, or I feel this pressure in my chest, and then I just want to get away from the thought or stop talking about it. I’m sorry, I know that’s not a very clean answer.

Losing interest in things… I haven’t really noticed that specifically. I’ve been so preoccupied with trying to get through the day and not snap at people that I don’t know if I’ve paid attention to what I’m enjoying or not enjoying. So… I guess I’m not sure, but nothing stands out to me like, “I don’t care about anything anymore.” It’s mostly that I don’t feel like myself.
Have you noticed any symptoms like restlessness, trouble concentrating, or a constant feeling of tension since the fire?

Yes… definitely the concentrating part. I don’t know if it’s exactly “trouble concentrating” or if my brain just sort of shuts off, but at work it’s been really bad.

Like I’ll be looking at the inventory screen, or the schedule, and I know I’m supposed to be making some decision — who goes where, what needs ordering, what got counted wrong — and I just… stare. I’ll read the same line over and over and it doesn’t go in. It’s like my eyes are moving across it but my head is blank. Then I’ll suddenly realize twenty minutes have gone by and I still haven’t done the thing I sat down to do.

And that scares me because I’m usually pretty on top of that stuff. I mean, retail can be chaotic, but schedules and inventory are things I’m used to handling. Now it feels like even simple decisions take forever because I get stuck staring at them. I’ll think, “Okay, focus, just pick one thing,” and then I’m still sitting there, frozen, like my brain won’t connect to what I’m seeing.
Since the fire, have you found yourself having intrusive thoughts or memories about it, like flashbacks or constantly thinking about what happened even when you don’t want to?

Yes. That’s actually one of the worst parts, I think. It doesn’t feel like I’m choosing to think about it. It just jumps into my head out of nowhere.

Like, I’ll be doing something completely normal — picking up a pan, or just opening something on the computer at work, like a spreadsheet — and suddenly I’m right back there in my head. I can smell the smoke again, and I can see the kitchen filling up, and it’s like my brain goes straight to that moment before I can stop it. It’s not like I sit down and decide to remember it. It just comes in, really fast, and then I’m stuck with it.

Sometimes it’s only a few seconds, but it feels much longer because it’s so vivid. I’ll be trying to do some ordinary thing and then I’m not really with that thing anymore — I’m back in that kitchen, seeing it happen again. And then afterward I’m shaken up because it feels so real for a second. I hate it, honestly. I keep thinking I should be able to push it away, but it gets there before I even know it’s happening.
Since the fire, have you found yourself avoiding certain places, people, or activities because they remind you of what happened?

Yes. I mean… yes, absolutely. I’ve been avoiding the house as much as I can. Even saying “the house” makes me feel weird, like my chest starts tightening before I’ve even gone near it. I know I can’t avoid it forever, but every time I think about going there, I feel like my body just says no. I’ll make excuses or put it off, like, “I’ll deal with that tomorrow,” and then tomorrow comes and I still can’t make myself do it.

And it’s not just the actual house. It’s anything connected to that day. There’s this mortgage folder — just paperwork, nothing dangerous, just a folder — and I can’t open it. I can’t even really look at it for long. It feels ridiculous when I say it out loud because it’s just papers, but as soon as I see it, I get this tight feeling in my chest and I feel like I need to back away from it.

Even the herbs on my patio… I know that sounds strange. They’re just plants. But they’re tied up with that day in my head somehow, and I haven’t been able to go near them either. I used to just step out there and check on them without thinking, and now I avoid even looking in that direction if I can help it. It’s like anything that connects back to the fire, even indirectly, my whole body reacts before I can talk myself through it.
Since the fire, have you found yourself being more watchful or on guard, like you’re expecting something bad to happen again?

I’m… not sure. I don’t know if I’d call it being “on guard,” exactly.

I mean, I feel tense a lot, but when you say it like expecting something bad to happen again, I don’t know if that’s what it is. I haven’t really noticed myself, like, scanning every room or checking exits or anything like that. At least not that I’m aware of. It’s more that I get uneasy, and then I don’t always know what to do with that feeling.

So… maybe a little? But I can’t honestly say I’ve been walking around constantly expecting another fire or something. I don’t want to overstate it. I think I’ve been more uncomfortable and shaken than actively watchful, if that makes sense.
Since the fire, have you ever felt detached from yourself or like you were watching yourself from outside your body, especially during those moments when the memories come back?

Yes… yes, that has happened. It’s hard to explain without sounding kind of strange, but sometimes when I’m walking through the store, it feels like I’m not fully inside myself. Like I’m watching myself from a few feet away, almost.

I’ll be moving down an aisle or talking to a customer, and I know I’m there — I know logically that I’m the one walking, I’m the one answering them — but it feels automatic, like my body is just doing the motions and I’m a little removed from it. The shelves and the lights and the customers are all there, but they don’t feel quite real for a moment. Everything feels sort of distant or flat, like I’m behind glass or something.

And it can happen especially when something sets off a memory, but sometimes it’s more like I notice afterward that I’ve been moving through the store without really feeling present. It scares me because I’ll think, “What is wrong with me? Why does everything feel unreal?” I don’t feel like I’m going to faint or anything, it’s more like I’m disconnected, like I’m watching myself get through the moment instead of actually being in it.
Since the fire, have you noticed any strong physical reactions—like a racing heart, sweating, or shaking—when something reminds you of the event?

Yes… I mean, the main thing I notice is my chest. It tightens up so fast, before I even have time to think it through. Like with the house — if I know I have to go near it, or even if I’m just thinking about going there, my chest gets tight and I feel like I can’t make myself do it. I start looking for ways around it, like maybe I can go another day, or maybe I don’t really need to deal with it right now.

And it’s happened with smaller things too, which makes me feel kind of embarrassed because they’re not dangerous. The mortgage folder, for example. It’s just paperwork, but if I see it or think about opening it, I get that same tight feeling, like my body is telling me to back away. I’ll move it somewhere else or just leave it sitting there because I can’t make myself touch it.

Even the herbs on my patio… I know that sounds odd. They’re just plants, and I used to take care of them without even thinking. But now they’re connected to that day in my mind, and I avoid going near them. If I look that way, I feel my chest start to tighten, and then I just turn away. So yes, there’s definitely a physical reaction, especially that tightness, and it makes me avoid anything tied to the fire.

It’s just paperwork, but if I see it or think about opening it, I get that same tight feeling, like my body is telling me to back away. I’ll move it somewhere else or just leave it sitting there because I can’t make myself touch it.

Even the herbs on my patio… I know that sounds odd. They’re just plants, and I used to take care of them without even thinking. But now they’re connected to that day in my mind, and I avoid going near them. If I look that way, I feel my chest start to tighten, and then I just turn away. So yes, there’s definitely a physical reaction, especially that tightness, and it makes me avoid anything tied to the fire.
